tagline: A former through highway becomes a nighttime road of lights and resorts.
intro: On the Las Vegas Strip, the roadside landscape consists of casino resorts, huge video signs and lights. FHWA lists this 4.5-mile stretch of Las Vegas Boulevard as an All-American Road and calls it one of the country’s few nighttime byways. The agency allows 30 minutes for the drive and several hours to enjoy the byway, emphasizing its history and roadside character.

The boulevard formerly carried U.S. 91, the main highway between Los Angeles and Salt Lake City. El Rancho Vegas opened in 1941 as the Strip’s first full-service casino resort; its success helped bring another hotel the following year. When Las Vegas sought annexation in 1950, casino executives led by the Flamingo’s Gus Greenbaum lobbied county commissioners for town status. The eventual creation of Paradise and Winchester kept the Strip in unincorporated communities. Construction of I-15 changed the boulevard from a through route to a street serving local residents and visitors. The Las Vegas Boulevard name has been in effect since 1959.

Traveling south, Sahara Avenue marks the departure from the City of Las Vegas, with the Sahara resort anchoring the Strip’s northern end. Continue along the boulevard past the Flamingo toward Mandalay Bay, the southernmost resort in the traditional Strip definition. Beyond Russell Road, the Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign stands in the median beside the airport’s western edge.

moments.title: Sahara
moments.text: The Sahara’s name returned after an eight-year absence. Opened in 1952 as the Strip’s sixth resort, it expanded upward with hotel towers designed by Martin Stern Jr. A 14-story tower opened in 1960, followed by a 24-story tower in 1963. A renovation begun in 1996 demolished the original poolside motel structures, another break between the early resort and its later form. The resort closed in 2011 and reopened after renovation as SLS Las Vegas in 2014. In 2019, another renovation restored the Sahara name. The property anchors the Strip’s north end at Sahara Avenue.

moments.title: Flamingo Las Vegas
moments.text: The Flamingo’s long operating history does not mean its original hotel survives. Billy Wilkerson proposed the resort, but financing brought in partners including Benjamin “Bugsy” Siegel, who took control of the project. The casino opened in December 1946, followed by the three-story hotel in March 1947. High-rise additions began opening in 1978. In 1993, the three-story hotel, the last original structure, was demolished to help make room for the final tower addition. Part of the property became a pool area and animal habitat with flamingos. It remains the Strip’s oldest continuously operating resort, despite those changes in its buildings.

moments.title: Welcome to Fabulous Las Vegas sign
moments.text: The circles spelling “Welcome” represent silver dollars, a reference to Nevada’s Silver State nickname. Betty Willis designed the sign, which Western Neon installed in 1959 under contract with Clark County. Its stretched diamond sits on two flat poles beneath an eight-pointed star. The greeting faces south; the north side asks drivers to drive carefully and come back soon. The sign entered the National Register of Historic Places in 2009. A 2008 project added a parking area and paved walkway to the median, creating official public access to the sign for the first time.
moments.notice: The white circles across the top are designed as silver dollars.
